assessment_scope: The Ω(log n) memory lower bound for a single deterministic agent in edge-colored graphs. Covers fully regular graphs, the periodic color sequence, and folding to close a loop. Excludes the maze/pebble history.

atoms.statement: A trap for a deterministic exploration algorithm is an edge-colored graph together with an initial location $v_0$ such that the algorithm, when started at $v_0$, never visits all vertices of the graph.

evidence.text: A trap for an exploration algorithm is given by an edge-colored graph G together with an initial location v0, such that the algorithm never visits all vertices of G when starting at v0.

atoms.statement: An agent with insufficient memory can fail to explore a graph in finite time essentially only by getting trapped in periodic behavior that forces it to move eternally on a closed tour without having visited all vertices.

evidence.text: The Space Complexity of Undirected Graph Exploration

To approach the question of how much memory is necessary in general to deterministi- cally explore a graph G of size n, we ﬁrst need to realize how insufﬁcient memory can manifest itself in terms of the inability of the agent to explore: Essentially, the only way that the agent may fail to explore G in ﬁnite time is by getting “trapped” in periodic behavior that forces it to move on a closed tour eternally, without having visited all vertices.

atoms.statement: The size of a trap constructed for a deterministic algorithm with a finite number $b$ of memory bits bounds the largest graph size that the algorithm can explore.

evidence.text: We ﬁx a deterministic exploration algorithm A with a ﬁnite number b ∈N of memory bits and construct a trap of some size n for this algorithm.
The size of our trap then bounds the largest size of graphs that the algorithm can explore.

atoms.statement: Because an algorithm with $b$ memory bits has at most $2^b$ memory states, it must enter some state a second time within its first $2^b$ steps, so its color sequence becomes periodic, $S=(c_1,\dots,c_{i-1})\oplus S_p^\infty$ with $|S_p|=j-i$.

evidence.text: To construct a trap G for A , ﬁrst observe that A has at most 2b different memory states at its disposal.
Since A has at most 2b different states, it must enter at least one state for the second time within the ﬁrst 2b steps.
Assume the same state is entered in steps 1 ≤i < j ≤2b.

Then the behavior of A and, consequently, S must become periodic after step i, i.e.,S = (c1,...,ci−1) ⊕S∞p , where ’⊕’ denotes concatenation of sequences, and Sp is a ﬁnite subsequence of S of length j −i.

atoms.statement: For a deterministic algorithm with $b$ memory bits, the trap is built as a fully regular graph of degree 3 with a fixed set of three colors, on which the algorithm produces the same color sequence $S$ irrespective of the initial location.

evidence.text: Our construction ensures that G is a fully regular graph of degree 3, using a ﬁxed set of three colorsC.
As observed in the previous section, A is sure to yield the same sequence S of colors for all fully regular graphs using colors C and irrespective of the initial location v0.

evidence.text: Assume that vi = vj.
Then, the algorithm moves on a closed tour of length j −i after step i while having visited at most i + j −i = j ≤2b differ- ent vertices.

atoms.statement: The trap construction yields a trap of size $n=O(2^b)$ for any deterministic algorithm with $b$ memory bits, which implies that $\Omega(\log n)$ memory bits are required to explore every graph of size up to $n$.

evidence.text: In either case, we have constructed a trap of size n = O (2b).

Since we can perform this construction for any deterministic algorithm with b memory bits, this implies a lower bound of Ω (logn) on the required number of memory bits to explore every graph of size up to n ∈N.

atoms.statement: The $\Omega(\log n)$ lower bound is tight, since undirected graphs with $n$ vertices can be explored deterministically with $O(\log n)$ memory via Reingold's result that USTCON is in L.

evidence.text: We will see that the lower bound shown in Sect. 3 on the memory needed to explore an undirected graph deterministically is tight, i.e.,undirected graphs with n vertices can be explored deterministically with O (logn) memory.

assessment_scope: Einstein-notation tensor multiplication, the expression DAG, and adjoint rules for multiplication and unary-function nodes. Includes why matrix notation is insufficient.

atoms.statement: Any multiplication of tensors A and B can be written in the generalized Einstein notation as $C[s_3] = \sum_{(s_1\cup s_2)\setminus s_3} A[s_1]\cdot B[s_2]$, where $s_1$, $s_2$, $s_3$ are the index sets of the left argument, right argument and result, and the sum runs over all indices that appear in an argument but not in the result.

The summation is over all indices that appear in at least one of the two multiplication’s arguments A and B and are not present in the result tensor C.

atoms.statement: Any expression can be represented as a directed acyclic expression graph (expression DAG) in which input nodes (no incoming edges) are the variables or constants and output nodes (no outgoing edges) are the functions the DAG computes.

evidence.text: Any expression can be represented as a directed acyclic expression graph (expres- sion DAG).
The nodes of the DAG that have no incoming edges represent the variables or con- stants of the expression and are referred to as input nodes.
The nodes of the DAG that have no outgoing edges represent the functions that the DAG computes and are referred to as output nodes.

atoms.statement: Matrix notation is insufficient for derivatives of vector and matrix expressions: for $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ the derivative is a matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, but the second derivative is a third-order tensor in $\mathbb{R}^{m\times n\times n}$ that cannot be represented in standard matrix notation.

evidence.text: Furthermore, when computing derivatives of vector and matrix expressions, even matrix notation is not sufﬁcient to express all derivatives.
For instance, for function f(x): Rn →Rm, the derivative will be a matrix M ∈Rm×n.
But already its second derivative will be T ∈Rm×n×n, i.e., a third order tensor, which cannot be represented in standard matrix notation.

atoms.statement: Even when a derivative is a tensor of order two, it may have no matrix representation; for example, when differentiating $f(x)=x^\top A x$ by the chain rule, the derivative of $x^\top$ with respect to x is not the identity matrix and is not representable as a matrix, though in Ricci notation it is the tensor $\delta_{ij}$.

evidence.text: And even in the two-dimensional case, i.e., when the derivative is a tensor of order two, it might have no corresponding representation as a matrix.
For instance, consider the sim- ple quadratic function f(x) = x⊤Ax, where x ∈Rn is a vector and A ∈Rn×n is a matrix.
When computing the derivative of f with respect to x using the chain rule, one has to compute the derivative of x⊤with respect to x, i.e., the derivative of a function that maps x to its transpose.
This is not the identity matrix.
In fact, it is not even representable as a matrix.
In the more powerful Ricci notation [39] it would be written as the tensor δi j.

atoms.statement: Standard Einstein notation, which omits the output index set and sums over all shared indices, can represent only a proper subset of the multiplications representable in the $*_{(s_1,s_2,s_3)}$ notation; for instance, it cannot directly represent element-wise multiplication.

evidence.text: In Ein- stein notation the index set s3 of the output is omitted and the convention is to sum over all shared indices in s1 and s2.
However, this restricts the types of multiplications that can be represented.
The set of multiplications that can be represented in standard Einstein notation is a proper subset of the multiplications that can be represented by our notation.
For instance, standard Einstein notation is not capable of representing element-wise multiplications directly.

assessment_scope: Quasi-threshold graphs as skeleton forests, QTM, the simple-path lemmas, and local optimality via path sorting. Includes the resulting linear-time inclusion-minimal editing and its streaming interpretation.

atoms.statement: In a quasi-threshold graph with skeleton forest T, an edge {u,v} exists if and only if u and v are in an ancestor-descendant relationship in T.

evidence.text: If u and v are on the same simple path, N[u] = N[v]: An edge {u,v} exists if and only if u and v are in an ancestor-descendant relationship in the skeleton T.

atoms.statement: Quasi-threshold editing yields a partition of a graph into communities and, for each community, a centralized nesting structure that is represented by its skeleton tree.

evidence.text: Quasi-threshold editing yields a partition into communities and in addition for each of them a centralized nesting structure repre- sented by their skeleton tree.

atoms.statement: Threshold graphs are the (2K2,C4,P4)-free graphs, and they form a subclass of quasi-threshold graphs.

evidence.text: Threshold graphs are the (2K2,C4,P4)-free graphs and therefore a subclass of quasi- threshold graphs.

atoms.statement: Incrementally inserting the nodes of a graph G into an initially empty graph with the QTM local moving routine yields an inclusion-minimal editing of G, because each step minimizes the number of edits.

evidence.text: With the local moving routine of QTM, we can incrementally insert the nodes of a graph G into an initially empty graph.
Due to Lemma 4, this minimizes the number of edits in each step.
Overall, this yields an inclusion-minimal editing of G, as it has also been shown, e.g., for interval graphs [26].

atoms.statement: Applying QTM to a node u on the skeleton forest with u removed and simple paths reordered so that the neighbors of u are at the top of their simple paths minimizes the number of edits incident to u.

evidence.text: Apply- ing QTM to u on T −which is T with u removed and simple paths reordered such that neighbors of u are at the top of their simple paths minimizes the number of edits incident to u.

atoms.statement: When the Quasi-Threshold Mover (QTM) moves a node u, in the induced quasi-threshold graph u is adjacent to the new parent v, v's ancestors, and the adopted children with their descendants. Each neighbor of u among these nodes saves deleting an edge, each non-neighbor requires inserting an edge, and QTM selects the parent and adopted children that maximize the number of u-neighbors minus non-neighbors.

evidence.text: In the induced quasi-threshold graph, u is then connected to v and all its ancestors as well as to all adopted children and their descendants.
Every neighbor x of u in this set of nodes saves deleting the edges {u,x} but every non-neighbor y of u implies inserting the edge {u,y}.
Therefore, we select the parent v and the children to adopt such that the number of u- neighbors minus non-neighbors is maximized.

atoms.statement: When QTM moves node u, neighbors of u at depth greater than $2 \times \deg(u)$ can be ignored, because connecting u to such a neighbor would force at least $\deg(u)+1$ edge insertions, whereas making u a root causes only $\deg(u)$ edits.

evidence.text: Consider a node v ∈N(u) with depth larger than 2 × deg(u).
If u is connected to v in the edited graph, this implies that u is also connected to all at least 2 × deg(u) ancestors of u.
Among these, there can be at most the remaining deg(u) −1 neighbors and thus at least deg(u)+1 non-neighbors.
Thus, this implies deg(u)+1 edge insertions.
Making u a root in the forest, i.e., deleting all edges incident to u, causes just deg(u) edits and is thus better.

atoms.statement: The one-pass streaming reading of inclusion-minimal editing requires that, whenever a node u is encountered in the stream, all edges between u and the already seen nodes are also supplied.

evidence.text: This inclusion-minimal editing algorithm can also be considered a one-pass stream- ing algorithm.

We only consider the edges of every node once, the only constraint is that when we encounter a node u in the stream, we also need to get all incident edges that are incident to the already seen nodes.

atoms.statement: Reordering nodes within simple paths is the only way a skeleton forest can be modified without changing the quasi-threshold graph it induces.

evidence.text: A crucial observation is that reordering nodes in simple paths is the only way the skeleton forest can be modiﬁed without affecting the induced quasi-threshold graph.

assessment_scope: Deadline-based speed scaling on power-heterogeneous processors. Covers the optimal-schedule properties (hypopower), the flow-based offline algorithm, and the AVR-based online competitiveness.

atoms.statement: In deadline-based heterogeneous speed scaling, m power-heterogeneous processors $P_1,\dots,P_m$ are given, each processor $P_p$ has its own power function $f_p(s)$ depending on its speed $s$, and job preemption and migration are allowed.

evidence.text: In [7 SPP,8 SPP] we focus again on classical deadline-based scheduling and assume that m power-heterogeneous processors P1,...,Pm are given.
Let fp(s), 1 ≤p ≤m, be the power function of processor Pp, depending on speed s.
We assume that job preemption and migration is allowed.

atoms.statement: Under general power functions, each processor's power function $f_p(s)$ is an arbitrary continuous and monotonically increasing function of the speed $s$.

evidence.text: General power functions: The function fp(s) of each processor Pp is an arbitrary continuous and monotonically increasing function of s. 2.

atoms.statement: Under standard power functions, each processor P_p has power function $f_p(s)=s^{\alpha_p}$ with constant $\alpha_p>1$, and $\alpha=\max_{1\le p\le m}\alpha_p$.

evidence.text: Standard power functions: Each processor Pp has a power function of the form fp(s) = sαp, where αp > 1 is a constant.
Let α = max1≤p≤m αp.

atoms.statement_raw: S1-3: Under standard power functions, each processor P_p has power function $f_p(s)=s^{\alpha_p}$ with constant $\alpha_p>1$, and $\alpha=\max_{1\le p\le m}\alpha_p$. (

atoms.statement: For standard power functions, some optimal schedule executes each job $J_j$ with a constant hypopower $Q_j=f_p'(s_{j,p})$. If $J_j$ runs on processors $P_p$ and $P_q$ at speeds $s_{j,p}$ and $s_{j,q}$, then $f_p'(s_{j,p})=f_q'(s_{j,q})$, which follows from the convexity of the power functions.

evidence.text: More speciﬁ- cally, if Jj is partially executed by processors Pp and Pq with speeds s j,p and s j,q, respec- tively, then f p(s′ j,p) = f q(s′ j,q).
Therefore, for any job Jj, let Qj = f p(s′ j,p) be the hypopower on processor Pp.
Property 1: Each job Jj is executed with constant hypopower Qj.

atoms.statement: The offline heterogeneous problem with standard power functions can be solved in polynomial time by a fully combinatorial algorithm based on repeated maximum flow computations.

evidence.text: As a main result in [7 SPP,8 SPP] we prove that the ofﬂine problem can be solved in polynomial time using a fully com- binatorial algorithm that is based on repeated maximum ﬂow computations.

atoms.statement: A schedule on heterogeneous processors is called an AVR-schedule if, for every job J_j and every unit interval I_t \subseteq [r_j,d_j), the total work of J_j executed during I_t on all processors equals the job's density \delta_j.

evidence.text: Based on the above algorithm variation, we say that a schedule S is an AVR-schedule if, for every job Jj and interval It ⊆[r j,dj), the total amount of work of Jj executed during It on all the processors in S is equal to δj.

atoms.statement: In the offline algorithm for standard power functions, feasibility of running all jobs at one common hypopower $Q$ is decided by a maximum flow computation. If no feasible schedule with hypopower $Q$ exists, the instance is partitioned into two independent subproblems, $(J_{\ge Q},P_{\ge Q},I)$ and $(J_{<Q},P_{<Q},I)$.

evidence.text: As we will explain below, this feasibility problem and the calculation of the corresponding schedule can be solved using a maximum ﬂow computation.
If such a feasible schedule does not exist, then (J,P,I) can be partitioned into two independent subproblems (J≥Q,P≥Q,I) and (J<Q,P<Q,I).

atoms.statement: The offline algorithm for standard power functions assumes that every job density satisfies $\delta_j \ge \max_{p,q}(\alpha_p/\alpha_q)^{1/(\alpha_q-1)}$; under this assumption an optimal schedule has all speeds $s_{j,p}\ge 1$, which allows the processors to be ordered from cheaper to more expensive.

atoms.statement: A kernelization for a parameterized problem $L$ is a polynomial-time procedure that maps an instance $(x,k)$ to an instance $(x',k')$ such that $(x',k')\in L \Leftrightarrow (x,k)\in L$ and $|x'|+k' \le f(k)$, where $f$ is a computable function.

evidence.text: More formally, given an binary encoded instance (x,k) ∈{0,1}∗× N of some parameterized problem L, a kernelization for L produces an instance (x′,k′) in polynomial time that satisﬁes: (x′,k′) ∈L ⇔(x,k) ∈L and |x′|+ k′ ≤f(k) where f is a computable function.

atoms.statement: Branch-and-reduce algorithms are exact algorithms for parameterized problems that combine data reductions with branching.

atoms.statement: Data reduction rules reduce the size of a graph while retaining the ability to compute an optimal solution.

atoms.statement: The degree-1 reduction for maximum independent set removes a degree-1 vertex $v$ together with its neighbor $w$. This is correct because some maximum independent set $I$ must contain $v$ or $w$ (otherwise $I\cup\{v\}$ would be larger), and if $w\in I$, swapping $w$ for $v$ gives an independent set of the same size.

evidence.text: We illustrate this by brieﬂy covering the degree-1 and degree-2 vertex fold reduction rules: (1) In the degree-1 reduction rule (see Fig. 1) one removes vertices v of degree one (and their neighbors), as they are always in at least one MIS.
To see this, note that v or its neighbor w must be in some MIS I, otherwise I ∪{v} is an independent set of larger cardinality.

If w is in I, one can obtain an independent set of the same size by removing w from I and adding v instead. (2) For the degree-2 vertex fold (see Fig. 2) one removes vertices v with exactly two neighbors u and w that are not adjacent to each other.

atoms.statement: A branch-and-reduce algorithm first applies reduction rules exhaustively, until no further reductions are possible or they are prohibitively expensive. It then picks an edge or vertex and branches into one subproblem per possible state of that element. It continues reducing and branching in each subproblem and returns the best result over all branches.

evidence.text: First, the algorithm aims to reduce the graph size by exhaustively applying reduction rules until there are no further data reductions possible or they are prohibitively expensive.

Then, the algorithm picks an edge e ∈E (or a vertex v ∈V, depending on the problem) and branches the problem into multiple subproblems, one subproblem for each potential state of e in regard to the problem.
The branch-and-reduce algorithm then continues to apply reduction rules to both of these subproblems and continues branching when there are no further reductions possible.
The branch-and-reduce algorithm returns the best result over all branches.

atoms.statement: In the degree-2 vertex fold for maximum independent set, a vertex $v$ with exactly two non-adjacent neighbors $u$ and $w$ is replaced by a new vertex $v'$ connected to the union of the neighborhoods of $u$ and $w$, which reduces the graph by two vertices. A solution is lifted back as $I=(I'\setminus\{v'\})\cup\{u,w\}$ if $v'\in I'$, and otherwise as $I=(I'\setminus\{v'\})\cup\{v\}$.

evidence.text: If w is in I, one can obtain an independent set of the same size by removing w from I and adding v instead. (2) For the degree-2 vertex fold (see Fig. 2) one removes vertices v with exactly two neighbors u and w that are not adjacent to each other.
In this case a new vertex v′ is inserted and connected to the union of the neighborhoods of u and w yielding a reduction of the graph size by two vertices.
Finally, if v′ is part of an MIS I′ of the reduced graph, then I = (I′ \ {v′}) ∪{u,w} is an MIS of the original graph.
Otherwise, I = (I′ \{v′})∪{v} is an MIS of the original graph.

atoms.statement: The suffix array (SA) of a text $T$ of length $n$ is a permutation of $[0,n)$ such that $T[SA[i],n) < T[SA[j],n)$ for all $0 \le i < j < n$, so it lists all suffixes of $T$ in lexicographic order.

atoms.statement: The longest common prefix (LCP) array stores the lengths of the longest common prefixes of lexicographically consecutive suffixes, with $LCP[0]=0$ and $LCP[i]=\max\{\ell\ge 0: T[SA[i],SA[i]+\ell)=T[SA[i-1],SA[i-1]+\ell)\}$.

evidence.text: It contains the lengths of the longest common preﬁxes of lexicographically consecutive sufﬁxes.

atoms.statement: Prefix doubling sorts suffixes by the $h$-order, which compares only the first $h$ characters. In iteration $k$ it computes the $2^k$-ranks from the $2^{k-1}$-ranks of $T[i,i+2^{k-1})$ and $T[i+2^{k-1},i+2^k)$. It stops when all ranks are unique, at which point each rank is the suffix's position in the SA.

evidence.text: The idea of preﬁx doubling [150] is to sort all sufﬁxes based on the h-order ≤h, deﬁned by T[i,n) ≤h T[j,n) ⇔T[i,i + h) ≤ T[j, j + h) (=h and <h are deﬁned analogously).

Now, during the k-th iteration, we compute the 2k-ranks using the 2k−1-ranks: for all sufﬁxes T[i,n), we use the ranks of T[i,i +2k−1) and T[i +2k−1,i +2k), which are known from the previous iteration.
We stop when ranks are unique; then, each rank is the position of that sufﬁx in the SA.

atoms.statement: External-memory induced sorting algorithms work in three steps. They classify all suffixes into two classes in a single scan of the text. They sort at most $n/2$ special suffixes, namely suffixes from one class that are adjacent in text order to a suffix of the other class. They then induce the lexicographic order of all remaining suffixes using an external-memory priority queue.

evidence.text: The general idea of all EM induced sorting sufﬁx sorting algorithms is to: (1) classify all sufﬁxes into two classes, which can be done in a single scan of the text, (2) sort at most n/2 special sufﬁxes, which are sufﬁxes from one of the classes that are (in text order) next to a sufﬁx from the other class, and (3) induce the lexicographical order of all other sufﬁxes using an EM priority queue.

atoms.statement: The DC3 difference-cover algorithm first computes $SA_{12}$ for the suffixes starting at positions not divisible by 3. It does this by treating three characters as one and recursing until all characters are unique. It then computes $SA_0$ of the remaining suffixes using $SA_{12}$ and merges $SA_0$ and $SA_{12}$ into the final SA.

Then, the SA0 of all other sufﬁxes is computed using the already computed SA12.
To obtain the ﬁnal SA, SA0 and SA12 are merged.

atoms.statement: In the Barabási–Albert (BA) model, one starts from a seed graph $G_0$ with $n_0$ vertices and $m_0$ edges and adds $n-n_0$ nodes one at a time. atoms.statement: In the BA model, each node of degree $k$ appears exactly $k$ times in the edge list produced so far. Dynamic weighted sampling therefore reduces to uniformly selecting entries from the edge list, which yields the linear-time generator BB-BA.

atoms.statement: In CA-BA, a shared random hash function $h(\cdot)$ with $h(i)<i$ is used, and the neighbor stored at position $i$ of the conceptual edge list is conceptually copied from position $j=h(i)$. If $j\ge 2m_0$ and $j$ is odd, the copy recurses on $j'=h(h(i))$.

If j ≥2m0 and j is odd, we retrace the sampling carried out.

atoms.statement: A CWA-solution for a source instance $S$ under a schema mapping $M$ is a solution $T$ in which every atom is justified by $M$ and $S$, each justification is used at most once, and every true positive statement (Boolean conjunctive query) logically follows from $S$ and the tgds and egds of $M$.

evidence.text: Informally, CWA-solutions for a source instance S under a schema mapping M are all those solutions T for S under M that satisfy the following properties: 1.
All atoms in T are justiﬁed in a certain sense by M and S. 2.
Each justiﬁcation for atoms is used at most once. 3.
Each “positive statement” (Boolean conjunctive query) that is true in T logically follows from S and the set of tgds and egds in M.

atoms.statement: For a mapping M defined by st-tgds, a justification is an st-tgd $\theta=\forall\bar x\forall\bar y(\varphi(\bar x,\bar y)\to\exists\bar z\,\psi(\bar x,\bar z))$ together with assignments $\bar a,\bar a'$ such that $S\models\varphi(\bar a,\bar a')$. An atom in T is justified if some justification and some assignment $\bar b$ for $\bar z$ satisfy $T\models\psi(\bar a,\bar b)$ and the atom is one of the relation atoms of $\psi(\bar a,\bar b)$.

atoms.statement: Consistent answering of conjunctive queries under primary key constraints is coNP-complete. Because relational queries have data complexity in AC0 and so cannot express coNP-hard problems, first-order query rewriting is impossible for the full class of conjunctive queries.

evidence.text: The data complexity of computing answers to relational queries is known to be in AC0, a complexity class properly contained in P, and therefore, it is impossible for a relational query to express a coNP-hard problem.

For instance, Chomicki and Marcinkowski have shown in [19] coNP- completeness of consistent answering to a conjunctive query in the presence of primary key constraints (i.e., one key constraint per relation), which precludes the applicability of rewriting for the full class of conjunctive queries.

atoms.statement: A configuration that is not bivalent is univalent, and it is 0-valent or 1-valent according to whether all executions starting in it produce 0 or 1 as the decision value.

evidence.text: A conﬁguration that is not bivalent is univalent, or more speciﬁcally 0-valent or 1-valent depending on whether all executions starting in the conﬁguration produce 0 or 1 as the decision value.

atoms.statement: A configuration $C$ is bivalent if there exist traces $T_0$ and $T_1$ starting from $C$ that lead to configurations $CT_0$ and $CT_1$ in which all processes decide 0 and 1 respectively.

evidence.text: The guidepost for this strategy is the notion of bivalence, where a conﬁguration C is bivalent if there exist traces T0 and T1 starting from C that lead to conﬁgurations CT0 and CT1 where all processes decide 0 and 1 respectively.

atoms.statement: The FLP result states that deterministic agreement cannot be achieved in an asynchronous message-passing system if even one crash failure is allowed.

evidence.text: The Fischer-Lynch-Paterson (FLP) result [FLP85] says something much stronger: you can’t do agreement in an asynchronous message-passing system if even one crash failure is allowed.1 After its initial publication, it was quickly generalized to other models including asynchronous shared memory [LAA87], and indeed the presentation of the result in [Lyn96, §12.2] is given for shared- memory ﬁrst, with the original result appearing in [Lyn96, §17.2.3] as a corollary of the ability of message passing to simulate shared memory.

atoms.statement: An initial bivalent configuration exists. If all initial configurations were univalent, two that differ only in process $p$'s input would both be $x$-valent, because executions with $p$ faulty are indistinguishable to the other processes. Chaining such configurations would make all initial configurations $x$-valent, which violates validity.

evidence.text: Otherwise, let C and C′ be two initial conﬁgurations that diﬀer only in the input of one process p; by assumption, both C and C′ are univalent.
Consider two executions starting with C and C′ in which process p is faulty; we can arrange for these executions to be indistinguishable to all the other processes, so both decide the same value x.
It follows that both C and C′ are x-valent.
But since any two initial conﬁgurations can be connected by some chain of such indistinguishable conﬁgurations, we have that all initial conﬁgurations are x-valent, which violations validity.

atoms.statement: If $e$ and $e'$ are steps of the same process $p$, the other processes can run a finite sequence of steps with no message from $p$ delivered until some process decides. That execution is indistinguishable to all processes except $p$ from the one starting with $De'e$, so the same value is decided in both, contradicting $Dee'$ being 0-valent and $De'e$ being 1-valent.

evidence.text: Now suppose e and e′ are steps of the same process p.

But now we consider some ﬁnite sequence of steps e1e2 . . . ek in which no message sent by p is delivered and some process decides in Dee1 . . . ek (this occurs since the other processes can’t distinguish Dee′ from the conﬁguration in which p died in D, and so have to decide without waiting for messages from p).
This execution fragment is indistinguishable to all processes except p from De′ee1 . . . ek, so the deciding process decides the same value i in both executions.
But Dee′ is 0-valent and De′e is 1-valent, giving a contradiction.

atoms.statement: In the case analysis, suppose $De$ is 0-valent and $De'e$ is 1-valent, with $e$ and $e'$ steps of different processes. Then $Dee' = De'e$, because in an asynchronous system one cannot tell which process received its message first. Since $De$ is 0-valent, $Dee'$ is also 0-valent, which contradicts $De'e$ being 1-valent.

evidence.text: Suppose e and e′ are steps of diﬀerent processes p and p′.
Let both steps go through in either order.
Then Dee′ = De′e, since in an asynchronous system we can’t tell which process received its message ﬁrst.
But De is 0-valent, which implies Dee′ is also 0-valent, which contradicts De′e being 1-valent.

atoms.statement: When steps $e$ and $e'$ belong to different processes, they commute, so $Dee' = De'e$. Then $De$ being 0-valent forces $Dee'$ to be 0-valent, which contradicts $De'e$ being 1-valent.

Let both steps go through in either order.
Then Dee′ = De′e, since in an asynchronous system we can’t tell which process received its message ﬁrst.
But De is 0-valent, which implies Dee′ is also 0-valent, which contradicts De′e being 1-valent.

atoms.statement: The FLP result extends to any asynchronous model in which it is impossible to tell which of two events happened first.

evidence.text: The FLP results extends to any asynchronous model where it is impossible to tell which of two events happened ﬁrst.

atoms.statement: The impossibility of agreement with one crash failure holds for the basic asynchronous model, and it can be circumvented by augmenting the model, for example with randomization or failure detectors.

atoms.statement: In asynchronous shared memory, operations on different locations commute, as do two reads. For a write and a read, or for two writes, only one process can tell whether both operations happened, so the same case analysis applies.

evidence.text: For example, in asynchronous shared memory, if e and e′ are operations on diﬀerent memory locations, they commute (just like steps of diﬀerent processes), and if they are operations on the same location, either they commute (two reads) or only one process can tell whether both happened (with a write and a read, only the reader knows, and with two writes, only the ﬁrst writer knows).

atoms.statement: In Paxos, processes are classified as proposers, accepters, and learners (one process may hold all three roles), and a proposer tries to ratify a proposed value by collecting acceptances from a majority of the accepters, with learners observing the ratification.

evidence.text: Processes are classiﬁed as proposers, accepters, and learners (a single process may have all three roles).

The idea is that a proposer attempts to ratify a proposed decision value (from an arbitrary input set) by collecting acceptances from a majority of the accepters, and this ratiﬁcation is observed by the learners.

atoms.statement: Basic Paxos is a one-shot algorithm that solves a single agreement problem, whereas multi-Paxos uses repeated executions of basic Paxos to implement a replicated state machine.

evidence.text: This is a one-shot version of Paxos that solves a single agreement problem.
The version that is more typically used, called multi-Paxos, uses repeated executions of the basic Paxos algorithm to implement a replicated state machine; we’ll describe this in §12.7.

atoms.statement: Paxos is a consensus algorithm that runs in an asynchronous message-passing model with fewer than $n/2$ crash failures, and the original algorithm does not tolerate Byzantine failures.

evidence.text: The algorithm runs in a message-passing model with asynchrony and fewer than n/2 crash failures (but not Byzantine failures, at least in the original

atoms.statement: In Paxos, after a proposer has received ack messages from a majority of accepters, it sets its value v to the value in the ack with the highest proposal number if any ack contained a value, and then sends accept!(r, v) to the accepters.

evidence.text: The proposer waits (possibly forever) to receive ack from a majority of accepters.
If any ack contained a value, it sets v to the most recent (in proposal number ordering) value that it received.
It then sends accept!(r, v) to all accepters (or just a majority).

atoms.statement: In multi-Paxos, if the proposer does not change often, the prepare and ack messages between agreement instances for consecutive operations can be skipped, reducing the time to certify each operation to a single round-trip of accept! and accepted messages.

evidence.text: If the proposer doesn’t change very often, a further optimization allows skipping the prepare and ack messages in between agreement protocols for consecutive operations.
This reduces the time to certify each operation to a single round-trip for the accept! and accepted messages, which is about the best we can reasonably hope for.

atoms.statement: Paxos preserves a value accepted in an earlier round because a majority of accepters that accepted it in round r and a majority that acknowledge in a later round r′ must overlap, so the overlapping accepter reports the round-r value to the round-r′ proposer, and by induction that value becomes the proposal value in all later rounds that get past the acknowledgment stage.

evidence.text: The second trick is to use overlapping majorities to make sure that any value that is accepted is not lost.

If the only way to decide on a value in round r is to get a majority of accepters to accept it, and the only way to make progress in round r′ is to get acknowledgments from a majority of accepters, these two majorities overlap.

So in particular the overlapping process reports the round-r proposal value to the proposer in round r′, and we can show by induction on r′ that this round-r proposal value becomes the proposal value in all subsequent rounds that proceed past the acknowledgment stage.

atoms.statement: In Paxos, a proposer first sends prepare(r) with proposal number r to the accepters, and an accepter replies with ack(r, v, rv) only if r is greater than both the highest proposal number it has already responded to with an ack and the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, where v and rv are the value and number of the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted (or ⊥ and −∞ if none).

evidence.text: The proposer sends a message prepare(r) to all accepters.
Each accepter compares r to the highest-numbered proposal for which it has responded to a prepare message and the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted.
If r is greater than both, it responds with ack(r, v, rv), where v is the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted and rv is the number of that proposal (or ⊥and −∞if there is no such proposal).

atoms.statement: Termination of Paxos requires that there eventually be some interval during which exactly one proposer is active and does not fail.

evidence.text: The solution is to ensure that there is eventually some interval during which there is exactly one proposer who doesn’t fail.

atoms.statement: Without additional assumptions, Paxos guarantees only its safety properties (validity and agreement) and does not guarantee termination.

evidence.text: We consider only the safety properties of the protocol, corresponding to validity and agreement.
Without additional assumptions, Paxos does not guarantee termination.

atoms.statement: Because a leader election mechanism of the kind Paxos needs for progress would allow consensus to be solved, the FLP result implies it cannot be built using only the tools of the asynchronous message-passing model.

evidence.text: Since implementing this kind of leader election allows us to solve consensus, the FLP result (Chapter 11) implies that we can’t build it using only the tools available in the asynchronous message-passing model.

atoms.statement: When there are multiple proposers in Paxos they can step on each other. For example, two carefully synchronized proposers that alternate sending prepare messages can prevent any accepter from ever accepting, because an accepter promises not to accept accept!(r, v) once it has responded to prepare(r + 1).

evidence.text: If there are multiple proposers, then they can step on each other.

For example, it’s enough to have two carefully-synchronized proposers alternate sending out prepare messages to prevent any accepter from every accepting (since an accepter promises not to accept accept!(r, v) once it has responded to prepare(r + 1)).

atoms.statement: A readable object type T is n-discerning if there exist a reachable state $q_0$, a split of processes $p_1,\dots,p_n$ into two nonempty teams $A_0$ and $A_1$, and operations $\pi_1,\dots,\pi_n$ such that $R_{A_0,j}\cap R_{A_1,j}=\emptyset$ for all j, i.e., after any sequence of these operations each process can tell which team performed the first operation; for readable objects $h^r_m(T)\ge n$ if and only if T is n-discerning.

atoms.statement: Registers, and objects whose operations are only reads plus non-returning read-modify-write (modify-write) operations that are interfering (any two either commute or one overwrites the other), have consensus number 1, because an FLP-style argument shows that no pair of operations can leave a bivalent configuration for a univalent one.

evidence.text: There’s a pattern to these cases that generalizes to other objects.
Suppose that an object has a read operation that returns its state and one or more read-modify-write operations that don’t return anything (perhaps we could call them “modify-write” operations).
We’ll say that the MW operations are interfering if, for any two operations x and y, either:
• x and y commute: Cxy = Cyx.
• One of x and y overwrites the other: Cxy = Cy or Cyx = Cx.

Then no pair of read or modify-write operations can get us out of a bivalent state, because (a) reads commute; (b) for a read and MW, the non-reader can’t tell which operation happened ﬁrst; (c) and for any two MW operations, either they commute or the overwriter can’t detect that the ﬁrst operation happened.
So any MW object with uninformative, interfering MW operations has consensus number 1.

atoms.statement: A non-trivial RMW object that returns the old value solves 2-process consensus when initialized to a value v with f(v) ≠ v: each process writes its input to a register, then applies the RMW operation, the first process sees v and decides its own value, and the second sees f(v) and decides the first process's value.

evidence.text: Suppose now that we have a RMW object that returns the old value, and suppose that it is non-trivial in the sense that it has at least one RMW operation where the embedded function f that determines the new value is not the identity (otherwise RMW is just read).
Then there is some value v such that f(v)̸ = v.
To solve two-process consensus, have each process pi ﬁrst write its preferred value to a register ri, then execute the non-trivial RMW operation on the RMW object initialized to v.
The ﬁrst process to execute its operation sees v and decides its own value.
The second process sees f(v) and decides the ﬁrst process’s value (which it reads from the register).5 It follows that a non-trivial RMW object has consensus number at least 2.

atoms.statement: Consensus numbers give only a partial picture of relative object strength: an object type with consensus number m cannot necessarily implement every object with consensus number m or lower in systems with more than m processes, as shown by an infinite family of objects $O_{m,k}$ all of consensus number m, where $O_{m,k}$ can implement $O_{m,k'}$ iff $k'\le k$.

evidence.text: The converse claim, that objects with the same or higher consensus numbers can simulate those with lower ones, is not necessarily true: even though a type T with consensus number m can implement any object for n ≤m processes (see §19.4), in a system with n > m processes there may be objects with consensus number m that T can’t implement.

In particular, a result of Afek, Ellen, and Gafni [AEG16] gives an inﬁnitely family of objects Om,k for all m, k ≥2 with the property that every object Om,k has consensus number m, but Om,k can implement Om,k′ in a system with enough processes if and only if k′ ≤k.
So consensus numbers give only a partial picture of the relative strengths of diﬀerent objects.

atoms.statement: Whether the $h^r_m$ hierarchy is robust for arbitrary deterministic objects is still open, though it is known to be robust for RMW registers and objects with a read operation that returns the current state, and for deterministic objects that do not discriminate between processes.

evidence.text: Whether or not the resulting hierarchy is in fact robust for arbitrary de- terministic objects is still open, but Ruppert [Rup00] subsequently showed that it is robust for RMW registers and objects with a read operation that returns the current state, and there is a paper by Borowsky, Gafni, and Afek [BGA94] that sketches a proof based on a topological characterization of computability3 that hrm is robust for deterministic objects that don’t discriminate between processes (unlike, say, single-writer registers).

evidence.text: If we omit the write stage of a read operation, we may violate lineariz- ability.
An example would be a situation where two values (1 and 2, say), have been written to exactly one process each, with the rest still holding the initial value ⊥.

atoms.statement: A partition argument shows that $f < n/2$ is necessary. If the processes are split into two halves with all messages between the halves delayed, a writer in one half must eventually return from a write because it cannot tell slow processes from dead ones. A reader in the other half must then return a value without knowing whether the writer's half is slow or dead, so the reader either misses the written value or returns it in an execution where the write never happened.

evidence.text: Split the processes into two sets S and S′ of size n/2 each.
Suppose the writer is in S.
Consider an execution where the writer does a write operation, but all messages between S and S′ are delayed.
Since the writer can’t tell if the S′ processes are slow or dead, it eventually returns.

Now let some reader in S′ attempt to read the simulated register, again delaying all messages between S and S′; now the reader is forced to return some value without knowing whether the S processes are slow or dead.
If the reader doesn’t return the value written, we lose.
If by some miracle it does, then we lose in the execution where the write didn’t happen and all the processes in S really were dead.

assessment_scope: The consistency condition requiring concurrent executions to match a sequential execution that respects real-time operation order. Covers handling of incomplete operations, linearization points, composability, and the contrast with sequential consistency. Excludes proofs for specific implementations.

atoms.statement: An implementation of an object is linearizable if, for any complete concurrent execution of the object, there is a sequential execution with the same operations and return values whose total order of operations is a linearization of the partial order of operations in the concurrent execution.

evidence.text: The strongest consistency property generally used is lineariz- ability [HW90], which says roughly that an implementation of an object is linearizable if, for any complete concurrent execution of the object, there is a sequential execution of the object with the same operations and return values, where the (total) order of operations in the sequential execution is a linearization of the (partial) order of operations in the concurrent execution.

atoms.statement: The partial order $<_H$ on operations in a concurrent execution $H$ is defined by $a <_H b$ when the response event of operation $a$ precedes the invoke event of operation $b$ in $H$.

evidence.text: The order in each case is deﬁned as a <H b if the response event for opera- tion a in execution H precedes the invoke event for operation b in the same execution.

atoms.statement: A linearization of an execution requires a sequential execution $S$ that meets the object's sequential specification, satisfies $H''|p = S|p$ for every process $p$, and satisfies $<_{H''} \subseteq <_S$.

evidence.text: Construct a sequential S such that S meets the sequential speciﬁcation of the object, H′′|p = S|p for all p, and <H′′⊆<S.2

atoms.statement: Linearizability can alternatively be shown by assigning each operation a linearization point between its invocation and response. The sequential execution $S$ is then obtained by treating every operation as occurring atomically at its linearization point, consistent with the object's specification.

evidence.text: An alternative method is to assign each operation a linearization point somewhere between when its invocation and response, and obtain S by assuming that all operations occur atomically at their linearization points is consistent with the speciﬁcation of the object; this is equivalent to constructing <S⊇<H since given <S we can always ﬁnd consistent linearization points.

atoms.statement: Linearizability is composable: if $H|A$ is linearizable for each object $A$, then $H$ is linearizable.

evidence.text: Linearizability has the useful property of being composable, in the sense that if H|A is linearizable for any particular object A, then H is linearizable.

atoms.statement: A linearization of a possibly incomplete concurrent execution $H$ is built in three steps: - Extend $H$ with zero or more response events to get $H'$. - Remove the invoke events in $H'$ that have no matching response to get $H''$. - Construct a sequential execution $S$ that meets the object's sequential specification, with $H''|p = S|p$ for all processes $p$ and $<_{H''} \subseteq <_S$.

evidence.text: implementation the ﬂexibility of deciding whether these operations have taken eﬀect or not, so given an incomplete concurrent execution H, a linearization of H involves three steps:
Extend H by adding zero or more response events, obtaining a new execution H′.
Remove any invoke events in H′ that don’t have a matching response event, obtaining a new execution H′′.
Construct a sequential S such that S meets the sequential speciﬁcation of the object, H′′|p = S|p for all p, and <H′′⊆<S.2

atoms.statement: Sequential consistency is weaker than linearizability: it requires only a sequential execution indistinguishable to all processes, essentially dropping the requirement $<_H \subseteq <_S$. That sequential execution may therefore order operations differently from the global order.

evidence.text: This says that for any concurrent execution of the object, there exists some sequential execution that is indistinguishable to all processes; however, this sequential execution might include operations that occur out of order from a global perspective.

(Essentially we are dropping the requirement <H⊆<S from the linearizability deﬁnition.) For example, we could have an execution of an atomic register where you write to it, then I read from it, but I get the initial value that precedes your write.

atoms.statement: Linearizability of an implementation can usually be proved using only complete executions when the implementation guarantees that any operation in progress can eventually finish. In that case any incomplete $H$ can be extended to a complete $H' = H''$ by running pending operations to completion.

evidence.text: Even better, if we are asking if an implementation of an object is linearizable—meaning that all executions of the object are linearizable—then we can usually prove this by proving it only for complete executions, since if the implementation has the property that any operation in progress can eventually ﬁnish, we can extend any incomplete H to a complete H′ = H′′ by simply running any pending operations to completion.

atoms.statement: Sequential consistency does not generally have the composability property that linearizability has.

evidence.text: Sequential consistency does not generally have this property.

atoms.statement: EIG gives a Byzantine agreement algorithm that runs in $f+1$ synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as $n \ge 3f+1$.

atoms.statement: Exponential information gathering (EIG) is a synchronous Byzantine agreement technique in which each process gossips, and its state is a tree recording who heard what from. The tree is built from pairs ⟨path, input⟩, where path is a sequence of intermediaries with no repetitions.

evidence.text: The idea of exponential information gathering is that each process will do a lot of gossiping, but now its state is no longer just a ﬂat set of inputs, but a tree describing who it heard what from.
We build this tree out of pairs of the form ⟨path, input⟩where path is a sequence of intermediaries with no repetitions and input is some input.

atoms.statement: Exponential information gathering gives a synchronous Byzantine agreement algorithm that runs in $f+1$ rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as $n \ge 3f+1$.

evidence.text: This technique was used by Pease, Shostak, and Lamport [PSL80] to show that their impossibility result is tight: there exists an algorithm for Byzantine agreement that runs in f + 1 synchronous rounds and guarantees agreement and validity as long as n ≥3f + 1.

atoms.statement: EIG achieves agreement through the notion of a common node, one where all non-faulty processes compute the same $val^*$. Every root-to-leaf path has a common node because it passes through $f+1$ labels and at least one is good. A node whose children are all common is itself common, so a non-common root would force a path with no common node, which is impossible.

evidence.text: Agreement: Observe that every path has a common node on it, since a path travels through f +1 nodes and one of them is good.
If we then suppose that the root is not common: by Lemma 10.2.3, it must have a not-common child, that node must have a not-common child, etc.
But this constructs a path from the root to a leaf with no not-common nodes, which we just proved can’t happen.

atoms.statement: No algorithm can solve Byzantine agreement with $n=3f$ processes. The $n=3$, $f=1$ case is impossible, and a protocol for $n=3f$ would yield one for $n=3$, $f=1$ by letting each of 3 processes simulate a group of $f$ processes that all share the same input.

evidence.text: Suppose that there were an algorithm that solved Byzantine agreement with n = 3f processes.
Group the processes into groups of size f, and let each of the n = 3 processes simulate one group, with everybody in the group getting the same input, which can only make things easier.
Then we get a protocol for n = 3 and f = 1, an impossibility.

atoms.statement: The Borowsky-Gafni (BG) simulation is a deterministic, wait-free algorithm that lets $t+1$ processes collectively construct a simulated execution of a system of $n>t$ processes of which $t$ may crash.

evidence.text: The Borowsky-Gafni simulation [BG93], or BG simulation for short, is a deterministic, wait-free algorithm that allows t + 1 processes to collectively construct a simulated execution of a system of n > t processes of which t may crash.

atoms.statement: In the BG simulation, the $t+1$ simulating processes solve a sequence of agreement problems to decide what the $n$ simulated processes are doing, and these agreement problems are structured so that the failure of one simulator stops at most one agreement.

evidence.text: The intuition for how this works is that the t + 1 simulating processes solve a sequence of agreement problems to decide what the n simulated processes are doing; these agreement problems are structured so that the failure of a simulator stops at most one agreement.

atoms.statement: The BG simulation assumes that all simulated processes alternate between taking snapshots and doing updates, so the actions of a simulated process can be determined by determining the sequence of snapshots it receives.

evidence.text: To avoid having to simulate speciﬁc choices of operations, the BG simulation assumes that all simulated processes alternate between taking snapshots and doing updates.
This approach means that we can determine the actions of some simulated process by determining the sequence of snapshots that it receives.

atoms.statement: In the safe agreement algorithm, a process sets its entry to level 1, backs off to level 0 if a snapshot shows another process at level 2 and otherwise advances to level 2, and then repeats snapshots until none shows a level-1 entry and agrees on the level-2 value with the smallest index.

evidence.text: When a process carries out proposei(v), it sets A[i] to ⟨v, 1⟩, advancing to level 1.
It then looks around to see if anybody else is at level 2; if so, it backs oﬀto 0, and if not, it advances to 2.
In either case it then spins until it sees a snapshot with nobody at level 1, and agrees on the level-2 value with the smallest index i.

atoms.statement: Because each simulating process is in the unsafe interval of at most one safe agreement object at a time, the crash of a simulating process can stall at most one safe agreement object and hence knocks out at most one simulated process.

It follows that each failure of a simulating process knocks out at most one simulated process.

atoms.statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ and a monomorphism $A\to B$, two maps $f,g:B\to X$ with $pf=pg$ are fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $A$ if there is a homotopy $h:J\times B\to X$ from $f$ to $g$ that restricts to the constant homotopy on $A$ and whose composite with $p$ is the constant homotopy $J\times B\to B\to S$.

evidence.text: For a J-ﬁbration p : X →S and a monomorphism i : A →B, we call two maps f, g : B →X over S (i.e., p f = pg) ﬁbrewise J-homotopic relative to A if there is a homotopy h : J × B →X from f to g which restricts to the constant homotopy J × A →A →X on A and composes to the constant homotopy J × B →B →S to S.

atoms.statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-operads, $p$ is a minimal J-fibration if for any two dendrices $x,y\in X_T$ that are fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $\partial\Omega[T]$ (fibrewise J-equivalent), there exists an automorphism $\alpha$ of the tree $T$ with $\alpha^*x=y$.

evidence.text: (a) Two dendrices x, y ∈XT are ﬁbrewise J-equivalent if, when viewed as maps Ω[T] →X, they are ﬁbrewise J-homotopic relative to the boundary ∂Ω[T].

(In particular, px = py and x and y agree on ∂Ω[T].) (b) The map p : X →S is a minimal J-ﬁbration if for any two ﬁbrewise J-equivalent dendrices x, y ∈XT, there exists an automorphism α of T so that α∗x = y.

atoms.statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-categories (or a Kan fibration between general simplicial sets), $p$ is a minimal J-fibration (respectively a minimal Kan fibration) if any two fibrewise J-equivalent $n$-simplices of $X$, meaning fibrewise J-homotopic relative to $\partial\Delta[n]$ when viewed as maps $\Delta[n]\to X$, are equal.

evidence.text: Deﬁnition 5.69 Let p : X →S be a J-ﬁbration between ∞-categories or a Kan ﬁbration between general simplicial sets.
(a) Two n-simplices x, y ∈Xn are ﬁbrewise J-equivalent if, when viewed as maps ∆[n] →X, these simplices are ﬁbrewise J-homotopic relative to ∂∆[n].

(In particular, px = py and x and y agree on ∂∆[n].) (b) The map p : X →S is a minimal J-ﬁbration (or a minimal Kan ﬁbration if p is a Kan ﬁbration) if any two ﬁbrewise J-equivalent simplices are equal.

atoms.statement: For a J-fibration $p:X\to S$ between ∞-categories there exists a minimal J-fibration $q:M\to S$ that is a fibrewise J-deformation retract of $X\to S$, and the retraction is a trivial fibration; the same holds for a Kan fibration between arbitrary simplicial sets.

evidence.text: Theorem 5.71 Let p : X →S be a J-ﬁbration between ∞-categories.
Then there exists a minimal J-ﬁbration q : M →S which is a ﬁbrewise J-deformation retract of X →S.
Moreover, the retraction is a trivial ﬁbration.
The same applies to a Kan ﬁbration between arbitrary simplicial sets.

atoms.statement: Any fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence $\varphi:X\to Y$ over $S$ between two minimal J-fibrations $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$ of $\infty$-categories is an isomorphism, and the same holds for minimal Kan fibrations between general simplicial sets.

evidence.text: Proposition 5.70 Let p : X →S and q : Y →S be minimal J-ﬁbrations between ∞-categories.
Then any ﬁbrewise J-homotopy equivalence ϕ : X →Y over S is an isomorphism.
The same is true for minimal Kan ﬁbrations between general simplicial sets.

atoms.statement: If $p:X\to S$ is a minimal J-fibration between $\infty$-categories and $f,g:T\to S$ are J-homotopic maps from an $\infty$-category $T$, then the pullbacks $f^*p$ and $g^*p$ are isomorphic minimal J-fibrations over $T$.

evidence.text: Proposition 5.73 Let p : X →S be a minimal J-ﬁbration between ∞-categories.
If f, g : T →S are two J-homotopic maps from an ∞-category T, then the pullbacks f ∗p and g∗p are isomorphic minimal J-ﬁbrations over T.

atoms.statement: For simplicial sets, minimal J-fibrations are readily closed under pullback, but for dendroidal sets pullback along a map $f:S'\to S$ of $\infty$-operads preserves minimality of a minimal J-fibration $p:X\to S$ with $X$ normal only when the induced maps of stabilizers $\mathrm{Aut}(T)_x\to\mathrm{Aut}(T)_{f(x)}$ are isomorphisms, a condition automatically satisfied when $S'$ and $S$ are normal.

evidence.text: In the case of simplicial sets it was rather evident that the class of minimal J- ﬁbrations is closed under pullbacks.

atoms.statement: The dendroidal rigidity result (any fibrewise J-homotopy equivalence over $S$ between minimal J-fibrations $X\to S$ and $Y\to S$ of ∞-operads is an isomorphism) requires both $X$ and $Y$ to be normal.

assessment_scope: Cover the three-phase mechanism of acute GVHD, counter-regulatory cell populations, and the supplied description of non-HLA genetic factors and epithelial target cells in skin, intestine and biliary ducts. Include the classical immunological prerequisites while preserving attribution and uncertainty; exclude clinical grading, diagnosis procedures, prophylaxis, treatment, study-specific findings, and a definitive explanation of organ tropism beyond what the source establishes.

atoms.statement: The pathophysiology of acute GvHD has been attributed to a three-phase process. Tissue damage from the conditioning regimen comes first, then an afferent phase of host antigen-presenting cell activation and donor T-cell activation and proliferation, then an efferent phase of effector damage.

evidence.text: The pathophysiology of aGvHD has been attributed to a three-phase process comprising initial tissue damage from the conditioning regimen which in turn leads to activation of host antigen-presenting cells by pathogen- associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) and activation and proliferation of donor T cells (afferent phase) and finally to the effector phase characterized by cytotoxic cell damage and release of inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1 (IL-1) and tissue necrosis factor-alpha (TNFα) that eventually produce tissue necrosis (efferent phase).

atoms.statement: In acute GvHD, the targets of the immune response are epithelial cells, including the basal and suprabasal cells of the epidermis, the intestinal epithelium and the biliary duct epithelium.

evidence.text: The targets of the immune response in aGvHD are the epithelial cells including basal and suprabasal cells of the epidermis, the intestinal epithelium, and the biliary duct epithelium, and the characteristic feature is identical, i.e., the presence of infiltrating immune cells close to apoptotic cells known as “satellite cell necrosis.”

assessment_scope: Covers event-by-event transport versus the condensed-history approach, the physical, physicochemical and chemical stages, and the role of cross-sections (dielectric formalism, phase effects, uncertainties). Also covers how direct and indirect damage are scored into strand breaks and clustered damage. Excludes the general Monte Carlo dosimetry method for clinical dose calculation.

atoms.statement: Track structure Monte Carlo codes simulate particle transport event by event, tracking the individual physical interactions, in order to reach the nanometric spatial resolution needed to link radiation track structure to biological effects.

evidence.text: However, in order to simulate the physics at the nanoscale and to possibly link it to the biological effects of radiation with track structure properties in the nm regime [54], an event-by-event tracking of the different physical events is necessary to allow for better spatial resolution.
Therefore, so-called track structure codes have been developed for applications in micro- and mostly nanodosimetry.

atoms.statement: Track structure is the nanometric-scale spatial distribution of all energy deposits (energy transfers) produced by the primary radiation and its secondary particles, notably electrons.

evidence.text: Indeed, in this context, it is necessary to “zoom in” on the scale of the target’s constituents at the nanometric scale to look at all the energy deposits (or energy transfers) produced by the initial radiation, as well as the secondary particles, notably the electrons.
This is the study of the so-called track structure of radiation.

atoms.statement: Track structure codes must include cross sections for ionization, electronic excitations below the ionization threshold and, ideally, vibrational or rotational excitations of the medium, in principle for all interacting particles but particularly for secondary electrons.

evidence.text: Indeed, in order to model all the physical interactions taking place in the physical stage, these codes need to include cross sections for simulating ionization, electronic excitations below the ionization threshold, and, ideally, vibrational or rotational excitations of the medium, in principle for all the interacting particles but particularly for secondary electrons, for the reasons explained in Sect. 4.3.2.

atoms.statement: Most theoretical models for the cross sections used in track structure codes are based on the first Born approximation using the dielectric formalism, in which the Energy Loss Function of the material characterizes inelastic interactions with charged particles and allows calculation of the mean free path and inelastic cross sections.

evidence.text: Nevertheless, most of the theoretical models for the calculation of the cross sections used in these codes are based on the first Born approximation that uses the dielectric formalism.
Here, the properties of a given material in terms of characterizing the inelastic interactions with charged particles are given in what is called the Energy Loss Function (ELF).
This function allows calculating the mean free path and thus the inelastic cross sections.

atoms.statement: Direct strand breaks are scored from energy deposits in DNA volumes, for example using an energy threshold of often 17.5 eV in the nucleotide backbone, or, in the PARTRAC code, a uniform-probability linear function from 5 to 37.5 eV.

evidence.text: From the resulting energy deposition values or interactions registered in the DNA volumes, direct damages are calculated using different approaches depending on the TS code.
For instance, in some cases, an energy threshold value (often of 17.5 eV) in the nucleotide backbone is used to define a direct strand break [30, 80].

Others, as in the case of the PARTRAC code, use a uniform probability linear function from 5 to 37.5 eV [81] in order to calculate the resulting direct strand breaks, taking into account that very small energy depositions from vibrational excitations can also lead to this kind of DNA damage.

atoms.statement: Because experimental Energy Loss Function data were obtained in the optical limit (zero momentum transfer), the function must be extended to non-zero momentum transfers using dispersion algorithms based on electron gas theory, which redistribute the imaginary part among ionization and excitation levels while keeping their sum consistent with the experimental data.

evidence.text: As the existing experimental data have been obtained in the optical limit (i.e., for a zero momentum transfer), it is necessary to extend the calculation of this function for non- zero momentum transfers.

Different dispersion algorithms based on the electron gas theory [53] are then used to redistribute the imaginary part of the function between the different ionization and excitation levels while preserving the agreement of their sum with the initial experimental data.

atoms.statement: Gas-phase atomic ionization and excitation cross sections, which some track structure codes use, are in principle unsuitable for low-energy excitations of valence electrons in water, because such excitations are sensitive to the electronic structure of the target.

evidence.text: However, still, some track structure codes use atomic ionization/electronic excitation cross sections [58] obtained in the gas phase even if, in principle, they are not suitable for low energy excitations of valence electrons in water, since such excitations are sensitive to the electronic structure of the target [54, 59–61].

atoms.statement_raw: Gas-phase atomic ionization and excitation cross sections, which some track structure codes use, are in principle unsuitable for low-energy excitations of valence electrons in water, because such excitations are sensitive to the electronic structure of the target. atoms.statement: Low-energy interaction cross sections depend on the state of the medium as well as its composition, so gas-phase and condensed-phase cross sections differ, and experimental cross sections for biological media in the condensed state are very difficult to obtain, with only a few data under specific conditions existing for liquid water.

evidence.text: An important point to consider is that at these low energies, the interaction cross sections depend on the composition of the material but also on its state.
That is to say that the cross sections are not the same for a medium in a gaseous or a solid state.
This leads to a particular difficulty because it is very difficult (not to say, almost impossible) to obtain experimental cross sections for biological media in their condensed state [24].

Only a few data obtained under very specific conditions exist for liquid water [56, 57] and these data are the basis for the set of models utilized to calculate the cross sections used by most track structure codes.

atoms.statement: Condensed-history Monte Carlo, which groups many scattering events into fewer artificial steps much longer than the particle mean free path with continuous energy loss, is used for dosimetry and most microdosimetry of very energetic particles but lacks the nanoscale resolution that event-by-event track structure simulation provides.

evidence.text: As we described earlier in this chapter, particle transport through matter using MC codes is generally handled via a “condensed history” (CH) approach [53], currently used for dosimetry and the majority of microdosimetry applications for very energetic particles.

In such a CH approach, many scattering events are grouped into fewer artificial steps, much longer than the mean free path of the particle, using multiple-scattering theories and a continuous energy loss along those steps.

However, in order to simulate the physics at the nanoscale and to possibly link it to the biological effects of radiation with track structure properties in the nm regime [54], an event-by-event tracking of the different physical events is necessary to allow for better spatial resolution.

atoms.statement: Condensed-history Monte Carlo groups many scattering events into fewer artificial steps much longer than the particle mean free path, using multiple-scattering theories and continuous energy loss, so it lacks the nanometric resolution that track structure codes obtain through event-by-event tracking.

atoms.statement: In split-dose experiments at 37 °C, cells continue through the cell cycle after the first fraction and reach a maximally radiosensitive stage. Survival therefore decreases as the time between fractions increases. At 24 °C the cells stay in a resistant stage, so their radiosensitivity stays constant between fractions.

evidence.text: At 24 °C, surviving cells stay in the stage of the cell cycle where they are resistant between the dose fractions and therefore their radiosensitivity is constant with time.

At 37 °C, they continue through the cell cycle after the first frac tion and at some time later will have reached a cell cycle stage where they have maximum radiosensitivity, whereupon the second dose fraction is given.
Consequently, survival as a function of the time between fractions will decrease with increasing time.
